basis: Original revision-note retrieval practice, reviewed against AQA 8525 first exams 2027. Study Rocket used as a coverage reference, not a source of verbatim questions.

updates.front: Explain the difference between data redundancy and data inconsistency.
back: Redundancy is unnecessary duplication of stored data. Inconsistency occurs when duplicated copies disagree. Separate linked tables reduce repeated descriptive details, while foreign-key values repeat intentionally to provide links.

additions.front: Why can a foreign key repeat when a primary key cannot?
back: Several records may link to the same record elsewhere, such as several loans belonging to one pupil. The primary key must identify each record uniquely within its own table.

additions.front: Why do repeated pupil IDs in Loans not automatically mean the database is badly designed?
back: The foreign-key values provide necessary links. The unnecessary duplication would be repeatedly storing all the pupil’s descriptive details instead.

additions.front: A pupil has three matching loans. Can their name correctly appear on three rows of a two-table result?
back: Yes. There is one output row per matching pupil–loan pairing. Repeated output names do not imply duplicate pupil records.

additions.front: Does SELECT remove unselected fields from the stored table?
back: No. It controls the query result. The stored table retains its fields and records.

additions.front: Why can YearGroup = 10 AND YearGroup = 11 not match an ordinary pupil record?
back: A single YearGroup value cannot be both 10 and 11. Use OR when either year group should qualify.

additions.front: Which condition includes loan durations from 7 to 21 days, including both endpoints?
back: DaysLoaned >= 7 AND DaysLoaned <= 21. Both limits must hold.

additions.front: Does ORDER BY DaysLoaned DESC put the shortest loans first?
back: No. DESC puts the largest duration first. Use ASC for the shortest first.

additions.front: Must a field used in WHERE appear in SELECT?
back: No. A field can filter records without appearing as a column in the displayed result.

additions.front: Why is a primary-key condition useful when changing exactly one record?
back: The key uniquely identifies the intended row. A condition on a repeated name or year group might match several rows.

additions.front: Write SQL to change only pupil 103 to year group 11 in Pupils.
back:
```sql
UPDATE Pupils
SET YearGroup = 11
WHERE PupilID = 103;
```

additions.front: Write SQL to remove only loan 501 from Loans.
Write SQL to show the book titles of loans shorter than 14 days, sorted alphabetically.
back:
```sql
SELECT BookTitle
FROM Loans
WHERE DaysLoaned < 14
ORDER BY BookTitle ASC;
```

additions.front: Write SQL to insert pupil 105, Noah, in year group 10.
back:
```sql
INSERT INTO Pupils (PupilID, Name, YearGroup)
VALUES (105, 'Noah', 10);
```

additions.front: How should the values in INSERT correspond to its named fields?
back: They must appear in the same order as the explicit field list, with suitable data types. The supplied primary key must be unused.

additions.front: How do UPDATE and DELETE differ when a WHERE condition matches a row?
back: UPDATE changes the specified field values in that row. DELETE removes the whole matching row.

additions.front: Does DELETE FROM Loans without WHERE remove the Loans table itself?
back: No. It removes every record from Loans, while leaving the table and its fields in place.

additions.front: Why should text such as Macbeth be quoted in an SQL condition?
back: Quotes identify it as a text value, such as BookTitle = 'Macbeth'. Unquoted names are treated as identifiers rather than the intended literal text.
